meaning: How far an index fund or ETF's returns drift from the returns of the index it follows, usually stated as a yearly percentage.
why: A small tracking error means the fund follows its index closely; a large one means it often does not.
how: Fees, cash held, and the timing of buying and selling shares all add to it. Compare it between ETFs that follow the same index.
formula: Tracking error = Standard deviation of (fund return − index return)
finlit: FinLit's ETF pages do not show it because our price data source does not publish it.

meaning: The total market value of the money a fund holds for its investors, usually in rupees crore.
why: A larger fund is usually easier to trade and tends to have lower running costs per unit; a very small one may be closed down.
how: Look at it together with the ETF's daily traded value, since a big fund can still trade thinly on the exchange.
finlit: FinLit's ETF pages do not show it because our price data source does not publish it.

meaning: How far an ETF's exchange price is above (premium) or below (discount) the net asset value of its underlying holdings on the same day.
why: It shows whether people paid more or less on the exchange than the holdings were worth that day.
how: Compare the exchange close and the NAV of the same day only; a NAV for a market holiday has no matching exchange price. Wide gaps are common for ETFs that hold overseas shares.
finlit: FinLit shows it only when the ETF traded on the day of the NAV published by AMFI.

meaning: The change in a price between two dates, as a percentage, without adding dividends or other payouts received in between.
why: It is the simplest measure of how a price moved, but it understates what a holder received when the fund pays out income.
how: Funds that pay out their income, such as many liquid ETFs, can show a price return near zero while holders still received money. Total return adds those payouts.
finlit: Every return on FinLit's ETF pages is a price return.

term: Liquid ETF (1-day rate or overnight ETF)
meaning: An ETF that lends money for one day at a time, for example to banks through overnight lending, and so holds very short-term debt.
why: Its price barely moves, so it is used to park cash, and the money earned is often paid out as a dividend.
how: Because the income is often paid out, its price return can look close to zero. Check how the fund house handles the income.

meaning: An ETF whose price follows the domestic price of gold or silver, and which holds the metal for its investors.
why: It lets someone hold gold or silver exposure through a demat account without storing the metal.
how: Its price moves with the metal price and the rupee, not with company profits, and the metal can fall as well as rise.

meaning: An ETF that holds government bonds, for example 5-year or 10-year benchmark G-Secs, and follows a government bond index.
why: Its price moves opposite to interest rates: when rates rise, bond prices tend to fall.
how: The longer the bonds, the larger the swings in price when rates change.

meaning: An ETF that follows an index built by a rule instead of by company size, such as momentum, quality, value, low volatility or equal weight.
why: Such an index can behave differently from a plain index like the Nifty 50 for long stretches.
how: Read the index rule before comparing: two factor ETFs can hold very different companies even when both are called equity ETFs.

meaning: An ETF listed in India that holds shares listed abroad, such as the Nasdaq-100, the S&P 500 or Hang Seng companies.
why: Its value depends on foreign share prices and on the rupee against the foreign currency.
how: Limits on how much money Indian funds may send abroad can make the exchange price differ widely from the NAV; check the premium or discount.

meaning: An ETF that follows an index of one sector, such as banks or IT, or one theme, such as defence or manufacturing.
why: It puts all of its money into one part of the market, so it moves with that part.
how: Compare it with a broad index ETF to see how much of its movement came from that one sector.
